title: token-index-cascade-rollback-walkthrough
content:
Summary:

This document captures the SRE investigation, timeline, and action items for the Token Index Cascade incident that occurred during a staged weight rollout on 2025-02-14. The canary cohort began serving a weight bundle that introduced a tokenizer mapping change (an internal token remap table was updated), which in combination with a partial incremental weight apply across variant groups produced a transient token-index mismatch. That mismatch propagated to downstream caches (edge KV cache + prefix cache), resulting in degraded decode accuracy and a sharp increase in customer-reported hallucinations for ~12 minutes in two regions.

Impact:
- Duration: ~12 minutes (2025-02-14 09:13–09:25 UTC) for primary spike; residual traffic anomalies cleared by 09:40 UTC.
- Affected: Canary region us-west-2 (10% of canary traffic) and small subset of dedicated pools with mixed-variant routing.
- Customer-visible symptoms: odd decoding (garbled subtoken sequences), increased error rates on structured-output endpoints for a handful of customers, and elevated latency due to retries.
- Metrics: token-level CER jump from 0.6% to 8.9% (p50->p95), average tail latency +120ms, errors (400/422) increased by 3x for affected routes.

How it was detected:
- Primary signal: automated quality guardrail (canary-eval runner) triggered: tokenization-consistency alerts (threshold breach) at 09:14 UTC.
- Secondary signals: SLO monitor p95 latency alert, and spike in support tickets referencing ‘weird characters’ and JSON parse failures.
- Oncall paging to SRE (Marcus) at 09:15 UTC.

Initial hypothesis:
- Suspected root: tokenizer mapping drift introduced in weight bundle + inconsistent model variant mapping in the rollout plan (not all nodes pulled the revised tokenizer metadata atomically).
- Alternative: edge KV cache not invalidated correctly after weight apply, so old token-id -> new subtoken mapping mismatch.

Timeline (concise):
- 09:05 UTC: Rollout of weight bundle v2025-02-14-1 starts (staged apply, 20% canary pool).
- 09:12 UTC: First canary-eval failures seen (small degrade on test prompts with token alignment assertions).
- 09:13 UTC: Guardrail fires; SRE paged. Brief investigation suggests decode anomalies; partial rollback started for subset of canary nodes.
- 09:16 UTC: Rollforward attempts to fix by re-applying tokenizer metadata to affected nodes failed (manifest replication lag observed).
- 09:18 UTC: Decision: full canary rollback for the bundle across region initiated due to risk of propagation to production pools.
- 09:22 UTC: Rollback complete for canary cohort (control-plane acknowledged), but edge caches still serving inconsistent prefix states causing residual errors.
- 09:25 UTC: Support mitigation: rate-limited automatic retries removed for affected routes to reduce duplication of bad outputs.
- 09:40 UTC: Observed return to baseline after cache TTLs expired and a targeted cache purge completed.

Root cause analysis (evidence-backed):
1) Tokenizer metadata change shipped inside the weight bundle without separate metadata-only deployment. The mapping reassigns several rare subtokens to new indices.
2) The staged apply split the fleet such that some serving nodes had updated model weights but stale tokenizer metadata (race in the control-plane manifest ordering).
3) Edge prefix + KV caches retained tokenization-dependent prefixes keyed by model-version string that did not include tokenizer checksum — cache keys matched old/new mismatches.
4) Manifest replication lag in us-west-2 (replication backlog due to transient S3 throttling) prevented timely metadata propagation to some replica hosts.
5) Automated guardrails detected quality regression, but the rollback path didn't immediately flush caches, allowing a short-lived cascade of bad decoded outputs.

Why prior mitigations failed:
- Staged apply assumed tokenizer metadata is backward-compatible; it wasn't.
- Control-plane ordering assumed metadata manifests replicate before weight apply; we relied on eventual consistency rather than strong ordering.
- Cache key design uses model-version but not tokenizer-checksum; invalidation logic did not trigger when tokenizer-only deltas were applied.

Short-term remediation executed during incident:
- Immediate: full canary rollback of weight bundle (09:18 UTC).
- Targeted cache purge/TTL reduction for affected edge nodes and KV cache (09:22–09:30 UTC).
- Disable optimistic retry path for structured-output routes (09:25 UTC) to avoid amplifying bad outputs.
- Temporary hold on further weight rollouts for 4 hours pending post-incident checks.

Post-incident actions (near term, owners appointed):
- A1: Separate metadata-only deployment flow and require tokenizer checksum verification step before weight bundle rollouts. Owner: Marcus Li. Due: 2025-02-21.
- A2: Add tokenizer-checksum to cache keys and invalidate caches automatically when checksum changes. Owner: Hannah Ortiz. Due: 2025-03-03.
- A3: Add a manifest-apply blocking check: control-plane should ensure metadata manifest replication to >=95% of replicas before weight apply continues. Owner: Owen Brooks. Due: 2025-02-28.
- A4: Expand canary-eval suite with synthetic prompts that exercise rare subtoken boundaries and assert decode invariants. Owner: Priya Nair. Due: 2025-02-24.
- A5: Run a backfill job to scan historical model bundles for tokenizer-integrity issues and report any risky bundles. Owner: ML infra team (TBD). Due: 2025-03-10.

Longer-term engineering changes recommended:
- Strong ordering for metadata vs weights: control-plane to implement transactional apply semantics for paired changes (metadata + weights) or require metadata-only rollouts accepted earlier.
- Cache-key hygiene: include tokenizer checksum and model-weights checksum, and provide an admin API to evict by checksum.
- Better observability: expose tokenizer-checksum as metric/dimension in canary dashboards and alert rules.
- Preflight validations: add a dry-run in staging that exercises a small replica set with the new tokenizer mapping and checks for decoding drift before global rollout.

Open questions (to resolve in follow-ups):
- Was there any customer-specific routing that caused a dedicated pool to see the bundle earlier than canary? (Investigate router logs)
- Are there older cache shards still holding long TTL entries that weren't purged? (Edge team to audit)
- Should we revert to synchronous manifest replication for tokenizer/metadata changes? Tradeoffs to be documented.

Communication notes:
- Customer comms: Support drafted a short note explaining transient decoding anomalies and that a rollback was performed; sent to impacted customers by 2025-02-15 03:00 PDT.
- Internal: Summary sent to eng-all and product with link to this doc and action items.

Lessons learned (concise):
- Tokenizer metadata is first-class and must be treated with higher deploy rigour (checksumed, separately deployable, part of cache keys).
- Eventual-consistency assumptions in rollout orchestration can be dangerous when pairing control-plane metadata with serving weights.
- Automated guardrails were effective at detection; the rollback cadence and cache invalidation needs work.

Appendix (investigation artifacts):
- Canary-eval logs excerpt (09:12–09:20 UTC): shown in attached gist (link above).
- Control-plane manifest timelines: replication backlog spikes correlated with S3 error bursts; logs attached in JIRA-INC-2387.
- Minimal reproducer: repo branch reproducer-token-shift in serving-runtime PR #1429.

Notes to self (SRE oncall checklist for next similar incident):
- Immediately capture: list of nodes that reported new tokenizer checksum and ones that did not.
- Before rolling back weights, purge or reduce TTL of token-dependent caches.
- If manifest replication lag > threshold, pause staging and escalate to infra.

Draft status and next steps:
- This is a working postmortem in review. Please add comments inline (Slack thread + PR) and assign any additional owners. WIP: finalize root cause section after infra team confirms S3 throttling window and replication metrics.
